sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: Immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is typically a monophasic condition with a variable onset after chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy. We report an exceedingly rare case of late-onset ICANS relapse, highlighting challenges in its recognition and management.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A patient receiving CAR T-cell therapy for large B-cell lymphoma was monitored for neurotoxicity. Clinical, neuroimaging, and laboratory evaluations were performed to assess symptom progression and guide treatment.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The first ICANS episode occurred 14 days after infusion, presenting as grade 4 ICANS with coma, requiring intubation and intensive care. The patient was treated with methylprednisolone and anakinra, resulting in full recovery. A second episode occurred on day 40, characterized by disorientation, confabulation, and focal seizures (grade 3 ICANS). Treatment with levetiracetam, anakinra, and dexamethasone led to resolution.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This case highlights the potential for delayed ICANS relapse beyond typical time frames, underscoring the need for prolonged monitoring. These findings support a possible biphasic course of ICANS, warranting further research on its pathophysiology and optimal long-term management.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy has revolutionized the treatment of relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL), providing durable responses in patients with limited options. However, it is associated with immune-related toxicities, notably cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS).

While early ICANS is well-characterized, late-onset or recurrent forms remain poorly understood. We report a rare case of severe ICANS relapse 40 days after CAR T-cell infusion, despite initial resolution with standard therapy. This case raises critical questions about ICANS pathophysiology, the need for extended monitoring, and optimal management strategies.

sec.title: Patient Identification and Clinical Course
sec.p: A 40-year-old man with LBCL (stage IIIs B, GCB-type, double-expressor, MYC FISH-negative, Revised-International Prognostic Index 2, Central Nervous System-International Prognostic Index 2), refractory to first-line R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy, was admitted for anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel) after a 7-month disease course. His history included mild intellectual disability with preserved function and severe obesity. After lymphodepleting chemotherapy with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide, CAR T-cell infusion was performed and the patient was monitored for CRS and ICANS. Neurologic evaluations, EEG, CSF analysis, and laboratory tests were conducted as clinically indicated. Inflammatory biomarkers included Endothelial Activation and Stress Index (EASIX) (lactate dehydrogenhase × creatinine/platelets), s-EASIX (excluding creatinine), and m-EASIX (with C-reactive protein replacing creatinine), based on their prognostic role in CAR T-cell therapy.

sec.title: Neurologic and Laboratory Assessment
sec.p: ICANS severity was graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy criteria. CRS was defined and managed per institutional protocol. Serial blood tests were performed to monitor inflammatory markers, including interleukin-6 (IL-6) and CAR T-cell expansion, to correlate with clinical findings.

sec.title: Standard Protocol Approvals, Registrations, and Patient Consents
sec.p: The study was approved by the University of Trieste Ethics Committee (26 February 2025). Informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the patient's death, and consent for publication was obtained from the next of kin.

sec.title: First ICANS Episode
sec.p: On day 3 after infusion, the patient developed grade 2 CRS with fever and hypotension, requiring 2 doses of tocilizumab (8 mg/kg on days 3 and 6) because of incomplete response. The m-EASIX score peaked on day 3 (Table). On day 14, the patient experienced a sudden neurologic deterioration, progressing rapidly to grade 4 ICANS with coma (Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy [ICE] score 0/10), requiring intubation and intensive care unit admission. EEG showed diffuse slowing without seizures; brain MRI was not feasible because of severe obesity (body mass index 55), but CT ruled out acute ischemia or hemorrhage. High-dose methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/d) and anakinra (100 mg every 6 hours) were administered for 3 days, leading to neurologic improvement. IL-6 peaked on day 4 (CRS phase), whereas CAR T-cell expansion (by flow cytometry) peaked on day 14, coinciding with ICANS onset (Figure 1). Immunosuppressive therapy was gradually tapered over 17 days, resulting in full recovery and discharge to the hematology unit. Prolonged hospitalization was required because of hypofibrinogenemia and opportunistic infections.

sec.title: Delayed ICANS Relapse
sec.p: On day 40 after infusion, the patient developed new-onset right facial clonus; nystagmus; and a brief episode of altered consciousness with behavioral arrest, orobuccal automatisms, disorientation, and confabulation. Neurologic evaluation revealed an ICE score of 9/10, with preserved cognition and language but impaired attention. Interictal EEG showed frontotemporal rhythmic delta activity with occasional sharp morphology (Figure 2A). Brain CT and fundoscopy showed no signs of intracranial hypertension while a direct CSF pressure was not measured. CSF analysis revealed pleocytosis (20 leukocytes, 95% mononuclear, predominantly CD3+ and CD8+ T cells), and extensive CSF/blood microbiological testing was negative. s-EASIX and m-EASIX scores peaked at 5.64 and 91.39 mg/dL, respectively (Table). PET/CT showed stable disease with partial metabolic response. The clinical picture was consistent with grade 3 ICANS relapse with focal seizures. Flow cytometry revealed a second CAR T-cell expansion peaking on day 40, coinciding with the delayed ICANS relapse (Figure 1).

sec.p: Treatment with levetiracetam (2 g/d), anakinra (100 mg every 6 hours), and dexamethasone (10 mg 4 times daily) led to rapid improvement. Anakinra was de-escalated after 19 days and stopped after 62 days; steroids were tapered over 2 months. Serial EEGs confirmed resolution of the abnormal activity (Figures 2, B–D). Follow-up PET/CT showed disease progression. Third-line treatment with rituximab-polatuzumab-bendamustine was considered but discontinued because of infectious complications under immunosuppression. The patient ultimately succumbed to disease.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This case highlights a rare and severe late relapse of ICANS occurring beyond the typical time frame, despite appropriate initial treatment. ICANS is classically an acute, monophasic syndrome that develops within 2 weeks after CAR T-cell infusion and typically resolves within days to weeks.1 However, rare relapsing and delayed forms have been reported,2-5 raising questions about its pathophysiology and long-term management. ICANS is thought to involve systemic inflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and CAR T-cell infiltration of the CNS.6 Severity and timing appear influenced by the CAR T-cell product and its costimulatory domain. In this case, axicabtagene ciloleucel (a CD28-costimulated construct) likely contributed to the severe neurotoxicity, consistent with data showing earlier and more intense ICANS compared with 4-1BB-based products.4

In patients with delayed neurologic deterioration after CAR T-cell therapy, differential diagnoses should include refractory CRS, other neurotoxic syndromes (e.g., tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity, cerebellar or fludarabine-related toxicity, stroke, or movement and cognitive disorders), infections, and disease progression.7,8 Diagnosing late-onset relapse is challenging. In our case, a comprehensive workup, including inflammatory markers, circulating CAR T-cell kinetics, lumbar puncture, EEG, and PET/CT, was essential for diagnosis.

The first ICANS episode followed CRS and IL-6 peak while the relapse on day 40 occurred without CRS but with renewed CAR T-cell expansion and a second IL-6 increase, suggesting IL-6–driven neuroinflammation. Tocilizumab, administered during CRS, may have contributed to delayed neurotoxicity by blocking IL-6 clearance and increasing its CNS diffusion.9,10 Siltuximab, an IL-6 ligand antagonist that does not raise systemic IL-6 levels, may represent a safer alternative, pending further studies.11

Although CAR T cells were not measured in CSF, 2 distinct peaks of peripheral expansion support CNS trafficking. CSF pleocytosis with a predominance of CD3+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes further suggests persistent immune activation within the CNS. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that CAR T-cell re-expansion, potentially triggered by minimal residual disease, may drive delayed neurotoxicity, even in the setting of immunosuppression.12
Limitations of this case include the absence of brain MRI and neuropathologic data, which prevent definitive exclusion of CNS disease progression.

This case underscores the importance of prolonged neurotoxicity monitoring, especially in high-risk patients. Continuous EEG aided diagnosis and treatment of grade 3 ICANS; persistent EEG abnormalities after clinical resolution support its utility for ongoing surveillance.13

Biomarkers such as EASIX have been proposed for early ICANS risk stratification.14 In our patient, m-EASIX scores peaked alongside ICANS episodes, suggesting a potential role in identifying at-risk individuals, although no biomarker is yet validated for routine use.

Anakinra has emerged as a promising treatment for severe ICANS based on preclinical models and early clinical data.14,15 In this case, anakinra combined with corticosteroids was effective in controlling both initial and relapsing episodes. However, while corticosteroids remain the mainstay of ICANS treatment, their impact on CAR T-cell persistence and long-term efficacy remains a concern, particularly with prolonged use.12

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: ICANS is a well-recognized complication of CAR T-cell therapy with variable severity, but delayed onset is exceedingly rare. This case of late ICANS relapse despite optimal treatment challenges the classical monophasic paradigm. Clinicians should maintain vigilance beyond the early postinfusion phase, especially in high-risk patients. Sequential monitoring of IL-6 and CAR T-cell levels may support early detection and management. Future research should refine CRS and ICANS treatment strategies to improve safety without compromising CAR T-cell efficacy.
